**[1] `host.id`:** Collecting `host.id` from non-containerized systems

**Non-privileged Machine ID Lookup**

When collecting `host.id` for non-containerized systems non-privileged lookups
of the machine ID are preferred. SDK detector implementations MUST use the
sources listed below to obtain the machine ID.

| OS | Primary | Fallback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux | contents of `/etc/machine-id` | contents of `/var/lib/dbus/machine-id` |
| BSD | contents of `/etc/hostid` | output of `/bin/kenv -q smbios.system.uuid` |
| macOS | `IOPlatformUUID` line from the output of `/usr/sbin/ioreg -rd1 -c "IOPlatformExpertDevice"` | - |
| Windows | `MachineGuid` from registry `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography` | - |

**Privileged Machine ID Lookup**

The `host.id` can be looked up using privileged sources. For example, Linux
systems can use the output of `dmidecode -t system`, `dmidecode -t baseboard`,
`dmidecode -t chassis`, or read the corresponding data from the filesystem
(e.g. `cat /sys/devices/virtual/dmi/id/product_id`,
`cat /sys/devices/virtual/dmi/id/product_uuid`, etc), however, SDK resource
detector implementations MUST not collect `host.id` from privileged sources. If
privileged lookup of `host.id` is required, the value should be injected via the
`OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` environment variable.

**[2] `host.ip`:** IPv4 Addresses MUST be specified in dotted-quad notation. IPv6 addresses MUST be specified in the [RFC 5952](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5952.html) format.

**[3] `host.mac`:** MAC Addresses MUST be represented in [IEEE RA hexadecimal form](https://standards.ieee.org/wp-content/uploads/import/documents/tutorials/eui.pdf): as hyphen-separated octets in uppercase hexadecimal form from most to least significant.

**[5] `process.pid`:** On z/OS, SHOULD be set to the Address Space Identifier (ASID), which uniquely identifies an address space within a single z/OS image. The ASID is typically represented as a four-digit hexadecimal value.

**[6] `process.args_count`:** This field can be useful for querying or performing bucket analysis on how many arguments were provided to start a process. More arguments may be an indication of suspicious activity.

**[7] `process.linux.cgroup`:** Control groups (cgroups) are a kernel feature used to organize and manage process resources. This attribute provides the path(s) to the cgroup(s) associated with the process, which should match the contents of the [/proc/\[PID\]/cgroup](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/cgroups.7.html) file.

**[8] `process.owner`:** On z/OS, SHOULD be set to the user under which the z/OS system software is executed.

**[9] `process.title`:** In many Unix-like systems, process title (proctitle), is the string that represents the name or command line of a running process, displayed by system monitoring tools like ps, top, and htop.

## zOS Service

**Status:** ![Development](https://img.shields.io/badge/-development-blue)

**type:** `zos.service`

**Description:** Refinement of the generic service entity for a z/OS system software service, providing z/OS-specific context for the service name and version.

**Attributes:**

| Role | Key | Stability | [Requirement Level](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/general/attribute-requirement-level/) | Value Type | Description | Example Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Identity | [`service.name`](/docs/registry/attributes/service.md) | ![Stable](https://img.shields.io/badge/-stable-lightgreen) | `Required` | string | Logical name of the service. [10] | `CICS TS`; `Datacom`; `ADABAS` |
| Description | [`service.criticality`](/docs/registry/attributes/service.md) | ![Alpha](https://img.shields.io/badge/alpha-mediumpurple) | `Recommended` | string | The operational criticality of the service. [11] | `critical`; `high`; `medium`; `low` |
| Description | [`service.version`](/docs/registry/attributes/service.md) | ![Stable](https://img.shields.io/badge/-stable-lightgreen) | `Recommended` | string | The version string of the service component. The format is not defined by these conventions. [12] | `5.6` |

**[10] `service.name`:** For z/OS system software, SHOULD be set to an abbreviated name of the z/OS system software.

**[11] `service.criticality`:** Application developers are encouraged to set `service.criticality` to express the operational importance of their services. Telemetry consumers MAY use this attribute to optimize telemetry collection or improve user experience.

**[12] `service.version`:** For z/OS system software, SHOULD be set to the version of the z/OS system software.

---

`service.criticality` has the following list of well-known values. If one of them applies, then the respective value MUST be used; otherwise, a custom value MAY be used.

| Value | Description | Stability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `critical` | Service is business-critical; downtime directly impacts revenue, user experience, or core functionality. [13] | ![Alpha](https://img.shields.io/badge/alpha-mediumpurple) |
| `high` | Service is important but has degradation tolerance or fallback mechanisms. [14] | ![Alpha](https://img.shields.io/badge/alpha-mediumpurple) |
| `low` | Service is non-essential to core operations; used for background tasks or internal tools. [15] | ![Alpha](https://img.shields.io/badge/alpha-mediumpurple) |
| `medium` | Service provides supplementary functionality; degradation has limited user impact. [16] | ![Alpha](https://img.shields.io/badge/alpha-mediumpurple) |

**[13]:** Examples include payment processing, authentication, and primary user-facing APIs.

**[14]:** Examples include shopping cart, search, and recommendation engines.

**[15]:** Examples include batch processors, cleanup jobs, and internal dashboards.

**[16]:** Examples include analytics, reporting, and non-essential integrations.
